headline: Is there an opening for Nvidia's competitors, now that Jensen Huang is out?
author: Kai McNamee

paragraphs.text: Nvidia has long been the kingpin of the semiconductor industry, a company whose huge technological bets paid off, making its chips the most in-demand chips in the world and crowning the company, for a time, the most valuable in the world. But with Nvidia's leader, Jensen Huang, out, does that leave an opening for Nvidia's competitors to catch up? We're going to put that question to Dylan Patel. He is founder and CEO of SemiAnalysis, an AI and semiconductor research firm. Welcome to ALL THINGS CONSIDERED.
DYLAN PATEL: Thank you for having me.
DETROW: So you and others have estimated Nvidia is probably a year, two years ahead of its competitors. With Huang out, can other companies catch up?

PATEL: I think that's the biggest risk at least. Over the last, you know, handful of years, Nvidia's lead has actually lessened, and so therefore, they've lost market share, albeit, the market has grown so fast, Nvidia's revenue and profits have skyrocketed so fast. But now, with, you know, many barbarians at the gate, when sort of Jensen is needed most, he sort of is disappearing or (inaudible) the game.
DETROW: Needed most by the company, the industry?

PATEL: I think most - the most to the company. The industry has for a long time tried to roll their own solution, you know, at least as far as the biggest customers. Google, Microsoft, Meta, Amazon all have been working on their own AI chips for, you know, a number of years. And yet, they all still relied on Nvidia. But their reliance is reducing to some extent, and that's their goal and has been their goal. And now, you know, the only way Nvidia can keep their market share and stay on top of the world is if they out execute everyone - right? - they keep innovating and bringing new technology to the market. But without Jensen, you know, the founder and the visionary of the company, it's going to be a lot harder for them to keep on top.

DETROW: One of the things you've written about that I think is really important to understand is the way that - like, sometimes I feel like a CEO's role in a company is overblown. But how much came to (ph) his personal decisions, his personal decision-making? Let's talk about this first on the supply side. How was his personal relationships with supply chain managers in Korea and Taiwan so key to Nvidia getting what it needed?

PATEL: There's no other company in the supply chain, including in the semiconductor supply chain, where the CEO is, every quarter, meeting with all his suppliers. And, you know, chips are such a complex supply chain. He has hundreds of suppliers. He's talking to every single one of them, going to Korea, going to Taiwan, going to China, meeting, having drinks with them, going to local fried chicken spots, or, you know, night food markets, everything to woo them. And given this is such a complex industry where, you know, products are improving by 2x a year - right? - it's at an incredible pace - you need your suppliers to have full focus and put their best engineers on your product. And this just keeps Nvidia ahead of everyone.

DETROW: I mean, a big part of the reason the company dominated this field the way it did was the really risky big bets that Jensen Huang took. Do you see another CEO taking those bets, or do you see another company trying to establish itself taking the types of bets that he took?

PATEL: You know, there's many visionaries within the company. The challenge is, are there visionaries who are willing to bet the entire company, right? Jensen with CUDA, the software that makes Nvidia what it is, he developed it in 2010, you know, and the company developed it in 2010. And everyone who was a technologist at the time, everyone who was on Wall Street at the time thought it was a waste of money, thought it was a waste of effort. And then it turned out to be the bedrock of all AI software. You know, is someone going to do something that is such a waste of money that, for a decade looks like a terrible bet? It really takes a visionary, and I don't know if too many people will make those kinds of bets. You know, if someone were to ask me, hey, Nvidia without Jensen, a decade from now, are they the one that's bringing the most important new technology to market? I'd probably wager no.
DETROW: Do you have any sense what some of Nvidia's next big bets could be?

PATEL: Yeah, so Nvidia sort of had this history where they started making chips, and then they started making servers, and then they started making systems. Nvidia now is really focused on the end applications. They're making - they're helping companies make medical devices. They're helping companies make satellites. They're helping companies make entire systems that include AI as a part of it. If they don't do this, then most small and medium-sized healthcare companies, and even many of the not - large-but-not-so-largest-ones can't afford to build their own systems out of AI.

And so I think that's where Jensen was heading - right? - was, hey, in automotive, in healthcare, in manufacturing, how do we make it so medium-sized companies, small companies can all start deploying AI throughout their businesses to make them more efficient, increase production, make their products better, make people healthier? Without that, only the biggest companies can do this. And then the profit motive sort of makes it so, you know, all of the profit is captured by a few, not diffused to the whole ecosystem.
DETROW: That is Dylan Patel, founder and CEO of SemiAnalysis. Thanks so much for talking to us about this.
